newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Clinton inaugural pales next to jamborees of old.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Clinton inaugural pales next to jamborees of old.

text.p: These modern U.S. presidential inaugurals, like the spiffy one planned for Bill Clinton, are very nice, of course, but they lack the wallop those rustic affairs of old used to have.
There was the 19th century jamboree when President Andrew Jackson -- a hero of U.S. wars against the British and the Indians -- fled his own riotous party through a window.

And there was the inaugural that killed William Henry Harrison a few years later, not to mention the one where George Washington created his own parade, right up America's East Coast. That was the first inaugural, in 1789, when one had to improvise.

The extravaganza due to start on Saturday and run through Clinton's Jan. 20 inaugural -- with its $31 million budget, its fireworks, $100 parade tickets and $150-a-head black tie balls -- will cater to the same love of pomp and need for inspiration that give those affairs their popular appeal.

They always aim to launch a new White House term with a gust of gayety, a dash of drama and above all proof that this president is a regular fellow who wants to share the fun with the citizens. (A notable exception was Ronald Reagan, who stressed formal inaugural swank and made no bones about it.)
Jimmy Carter actually called his 1977 event "The People's Inaugural."
So, you want people?

George Washington attracted a sizable chunk of the 3.9 million people in the brand new United States of America when he travelled by carriage, barge and horseback -- a white horse, they say -- from Mount Vernon, his Virginia home, to New York, the first capital, to take the oath as the first president.
Vast throngs turned out to cheer and fete him all along the route. Lacking federally provided fireworks, they fired their own cannon. The trip took seven days.

In New York he took his oath on a balcony of Federal Hall overlooking Broad and Wall Streets, gave the first inaugural address to a mob of thousands, went inside for a slap-up lunch and slept it all off at Sam Osgood's house on Cherry Street.
But Jackson may hold the patent on "people's inaugurals."

He ran in 1828 as a populist, a two-fisted frontier Indian-fighter and military leader. He was followed to Washington by hordes of the boistrous, whiskey-loving, backwoodsmen who had elected him, and when he completed his Inaugural Address and rode down dirt-road Pennsylvania Avenue to the White House on horseback, they traipsed after him.

According to accounts of the time, they gobbled up the cakes, ice cream and punch set up for a reception, slopped much of it on the floors, stood on chairs, tracked mud around, smashed crockery and crystal and had a great old time.

It has become lore that Jackson, brawler that he once was, enjoyed this primitive bacchanal. But in fact, he was then 61, ill and grieving over the recent death of his beloved wife. He himself was jostled by the revellers and, it says here in this history book, "escaped through a window."

Far greater calamity befell Harrison, yet another hero of the Indian wars, who caught a rotten cold while delivering a seemingly endless Inaugural Address on a chill, rainy day in 1841 and died of pneumonia exactly one month later.
That made him the shortest-serving president in U.S. history and the answer to a heartless trivia question.

He did, however, get to see the first inaugural parade by U.S. military contingents. That foreshadowed the miles-long televised parades that are now the centrepiece of the whole event for many Americans, with their baton twirlers, state floats, Elvis impersonators, giant rubber peanuts and so on.

Modern inaugurals have offered some drama too, none more so than the snowy 1961 event in which John Kennedy marked a generational torch-passing with his call to "ask not what your country can do for you."

Foreign crisis added high tension to Ronald Reagan's 1981 inaugural when Iran's Moslem revolutionary government finally released 52 American hostages, held since late 1979, minutes after he took his oath to succeed Carter. TV networks offered split-screen coverage: The inauguration on one side, the hostages' plane awaiting takeoff clearance on the other.
The Iranians refused to free them until Carter was out, in a vindictive gesture. Reagan was able to announce the news of their release, glass raised in toast, at a Senate luncheon.
His next inaugural in 1985 was unusual too: Arctic weather cancelled all outdoor ceremonies. That was a first.
Weather forecasting is a routine part of preparations for modern inaugurals. The current prediction for next Monday is 35-40 F (1.66-4.44C) and no precipitation. Nice, for January.
Harrison should have had it so good.
